html:
On 23 February 1944 the Soviet secret police began deporting the whole Chechen and Ingush peoples, close to half a million people, from their homeland in the North Caucasus to Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Chechens call it Aardakh, the Exodus.

Stalin and his police chief Lavrentiy Beria accused them of helping the Germans, who had briefly reached the Caucasus. About 100,000 NKVD troops carried it out in a few days. People were packed into freight trains; in the mountain village of Khaibakh, those who could not be moved were reportedly burned alive. In the first years of exile, in hunger and cold, a large share of the deportees died, a quarter or more by many estimates. The Chechen-Ingush republic was abolished.

They were allowed home only in 1957, under Khrushchev, and found others living in their houses. The memory of the exile fed the Chechen drive for independence and the wars of the 1990s. The European Parliament recognised it as a genocide in 2004. It was one of several deportations of whole peoples, after the Volga Germans and the Koreans, and alongside the Crimean Tatars, Kalmyks, Karachays and Balkars.
